title: Don't Trust AI For Blood Pressure Monitor Recommendations, Study Warns
source_used: American Heart Association news release (HealthDay reported the same study; its page returned no text)
key_facts: Researchers presented the study at the American Heart Association's Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026 (Arlington, Virginia, 7-11 Oct); it is an abstract, not peer-reviewed.
They tested 324 home blood pressure monitors (145 validated, 179 not validated) with four AI search tools: Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Perplexity.
ChatGPT, Copilot and Perplexity were right only about 63% to 83% of the time; Gemini was best at 86% to 91%.
All four tools were less accurate at recognising validated monitors than unvalidated ones.
When researchers repeated questions on a different day or computer, the tools often gave a different answer.
The authors could not determine why the tools struggled; a limitation is that results will likely change as AI improves.
Presenting author Anna Soriano, a resident at the University of Montreal, said most tools did only slightly better than a coin flip.
quote_evidence: Three of four leading AI-powered search tools accurately identified home blood pressure monitors that met validated clinical standards only 63%-83% of the time.
The findings are considered preliminary until published as a full manuscript in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.
People may unknowingly think a device is validated based on the AI tool’s inaccurate responses.
why_it_matters_hint: People asking chatbots which home blood pressure monitor is accurate may get wrong answers.
